Samson. An Israelite judge whose extraordinary physical strength made him a folk hero and champion against Philistine oppression.

Born under a special Nazirite vow that prohibited him from cutting his hair, his strength lay in his uncut locks, a sacred symbol of his covenant with God. He could tear lions apart and carry away city gates. He served as one of the judges of Israel, a period before monarchy when God raised up leaders to rescue the people from enemies.

He was betrayed by Delilah, the woman he loved, who discovered the secret of his strength and handed him over to the Philistines. His eyes were gouged out by the Philistines, and he was enslaved to grind grain in their prison. In his final act, blind and weakened, he pushed apart two pillars supporting the temple of Dagon, bringing the building down and killing more Philistines than he had killed in his lifetime.

His story emphasizes the tension between God's empowerment and human weakness, strength coupled with moral failing. His tragic life illustrates the consequences of pride and betrayal, culminating in his dramatic final act of destruction. His life is recorded in the book of Judges, chapters thirteen through sixteen.
